tweets.text:
Apparently the Wednesday rally came too late to save the AAII survey as American Association of Individual Investors (AAII), a retail focused weekly investor survey, edged more bearish:

AAII Bulls (those who see higher stock prices in 6 months, blue line) fell to 34.1%, the least in six weeks, from 37.8% the prior week (still though above the 28.8% seven weeks ago, which was the least since September 2025), and falling back below the long-term historic average of 37.5% after a week above.

Bulls also remained below the level of the Bears (who see lower stock prices in 6 months, red line), as the Bears rose to 48.4%, the most in seven weeks, from 41.4% the prior week (still though below the 53.3% seven weeks ago, the highest since May 2025). That leaves Bulls above Bears just twice in the last 16 weeks. Bears also remain above the long-term average of 31.0% for a 38th straight week (and they’ve only been below it 9 weeks since Dec 12, 2024).

The Neutral camp (yellow line) dropped to 17.5%, the least in two weeks, from 20.7% (just above the 17.3% two weeks ago, which was the least since early April). It remains under the long-run average of 31.5% and has been over that only twice since July 2024.

Challenger October job cuts the lowest for an October since 2023 at 43,994, +2% month-over-month but -71% year-over-year, and below the 56,348 average for October from 2015 to 2025. Through October 617,189, -44% and the least for January-October since 2022.

Note the year-over-year drop still includes last year’s DOGE reductions are rolling out of the base. Government is -93% year to date and DC alone is a 291,905 swing.

The bigger story may be the reason employers give has flipped:

▪️ Market/economic conditions led for a 2nd straight month at 16,407 (37% of the month) and at 130,531 year to date has now overtaken AI as the top reason of 2026
▪️ AI cited for just 1,265 cuts in October, under 3% of the month and its lowest of the year — after peaking at 40% of May’s cuts and leading five straight months
▪️ Demand downturn 6,118 in the month, 21,347 year to date, +145%
▪️ Group every economic-weakness reason (market/economic conditions, closings, restructuring, contract loss, demand downturn, bankruptcy, financial loss) and you get 92% of October’s cuts and 66% year to date

Andy Challenger: “The reasons employers give have shifted from technology to the economy… That is a more cautious signal, though the overall pace of cutting remains low.”

Sectors:
▪️ Food led with 9,677, its highest month this year, 39,370 year to date +43%
▪️ Technology 5,576, its lowest month of the year, but still leads 2026 at 171,501 (28% of all cuts), already past its full-year 2025 total of 154,445
▪️ Retail cut 3,692 in the same month it announced 13,300 hires
▪️ Not counted: Microsoft’s voluntary exit offers to 60,000 employees. Challenger only books voluntary programs when employees accept or a target is stated, so that’s an overhang on the next few reports

Tier1Alpha says Wednesday's equity rally was boosted by hedge unwinds: 

While there is no lack of interpretations of these relief rallies from a fundamental viewpoint, as usual, we approach them from a market structure perspective first. In this case, the common thread across these past occurrences comes down to the rapid unwinding of event-risk hedges, which can create substantial mechanical buying pressure regardless of whether the underlying uncertainty has actually been resolved.

We saw fairly clear evidence of this yesterday, with a sharp decline across multiple tenors of the volatility surface... Combined, these suggest that participants were aggressively reducing their demand for downside protection as election-related uncertainty began to fade.

...While the initial covering flows can provide a meaningful tailwind for equities, that source of mechanical demand is ultimately temporary. Once it has been exhausted, the market becomes increasingly sensitive to other sources of flow, which is essentially what we're left with today.

Some ammo for the doves. 

Productivity was the strongest since Q3 ‘25 (+4.5%), the sixth straight gain and the third straight acceleration. Importantly, the mix was favorable for the 1990's-style pro-productivity camp: output rose +3.7%, also the most since Q3 ‘25, while hours worked rose just +0.1%.

▪️ Unit labor costs fell for the first time since Q2 ‘25 (−1.1%) against an expected rise. They’re up +2.39% year-over-year (from +2.6%)
▪️ Hourly compensation +2.9%, the least since Q4 ‘22 (+0.9%), which echoes the slowdown in last week’s ECI
▪️ Real hourly compensation +1.1% after a revised −1.9% in Q2 (was −3.3%). Year-over-year it’s just +1.0%, the least since Q3 ‘23 and below its +1.50% long-run average
▪️ Productivity just +2.06% year-over-year, the least since Q2 ‘23, but still well above the +1.27% average for 2010–2019

Elsewhere:
▪️ Services (non-manufacturing) productivity +4.1%, the most since Q3 ‘25, with unit labor costs −0.9%
▪️ Manufacturing productivity +0.3% (durable +2.2%, nondurable −1.7%). Manufacturing unit labor costs +2.7%, and +4.0% year-over-year, the most since Q4 ‘24

Data from the BLS Productivity and Costs release.

Initial jobless claims came in at 189,000 for the week ending October 31, below the 196,000 estimate and down 6,000 from an upwardly revised 195,000. 

That matches the July 18 low as the lowest since 1969 and is only the 18th week below 200,000 since then. The four-week average fell 2,250 to 194,750, the lowest since September 1969.

Continuing claims rose 23,000, the most since February, to 1,718,000. That came though after the prior week was revised down to 1,695,000, the lowest since April 2023. 

Their four-week average is 238,000 lower year-over-year, the largest gap since December 2022, and has now been lower from the prior year's week for 40 straight weeks.

A couple of interesting posts in @C_Barraud's packed Thursday Brief indicate that while China’s stock rescue package got a shrug, as I posted on Tuesday, the US midterm results got a rally.

After Beijing rolled out its 2024-style support tools on Monday, the CSI 300 slipped 0.2% Tuesday and the tech-heavy Star 50 fell 3.8%. Then Democrats swept both chambers of Congress, and the CSI 300 jumped 2.3% Wednesday, its best day since July. It added 0.3% Thursday to 4,113, up 2.6% in two sessions.

Hong Kong followed with a bigger move Thursday:
▪️ The Hang Seng rose 3.7%, its best day since February 2025 (+4.0% on February 21, 2025, during the DeepSeek rally). It’s now up about 8% from its October 22 low.
▪️ The Hang Seng Tech rose 5.6%, the most since February 2025, per Bloomberg.
▪️ Alibaba and Tencent each rose more than 7%, and Meituan added 6.8%.

Investors are reading the result as a risk to the US AI hardware trade and rotating into value. China’s internet platforms are about as cheap as large-cap tech gets: Bloomberg notes the Hang Seng Tech traded at 13 times forward earnings last month, the lowest since 2024. Bloomberg Intelligence’s Marvin Chen sees three rotations at once. Money is moving out of Korea and Taiwan into China, into value after China was “stuck at trough valuations” while the rest of the world rallied, and away from “tech hardware and pure AI plays.”

The same rotation shows up in the US. Bespoke says 91.5% of consumer discretionary stocks are above their 50-day averages, the highest in at least a year, compared with 35.5% of tech stocks.

Positioning added fuel. Short selling was 32% of Hong Kong’s turnover on Tuesday, the highest in more than three years, according to Bloomberg. Lotus Asset Management’s Hao Hong calls the move “one of the biggest short squeezes in recent years.” The cost of hedging the Hang Seng Tech fell to its lowest since July, and options volume on the Tracker Fund hit a one-year high as bullish bets dominated.

To be fair to Beijing, Bloomberg also reported stepped-up national-team buying and buybacks Wednesday, so the policy floor is perhaps part of this. 

A caveat: Big up days aren’t reliable bottoms. Since 2000, the Hang Seng has had 53 separate days of 3.5% or more. While a month later it was higher 62% of the time (median +3.0%), three months later it was a coin flip: higher 53% of the time, with a median gain of 1.5%.

Citadel's Rubner: The election is over and markets are breathing a sigh of relief... This sets the stage for investors to rebuild equity exposure into year-end.

October brought a significant reset across Technology and the AI complex, but remarkably little broad-based selling… with investors rotating into other parts of the market rather than indiscriminately reducing equity exposure.

The underlying demand picture has also changed. Retail has bought US equities for 22 consecutive sessions (the sixth longest and fifth largest buying streak since 2017 - chart), corporate buyback windows are reopening, and CTA positioning has fallen to -3.3 standard deviations, leaving considerable room for systematic buying as markets recover. 

Meanwhile, earnings continue to beat elevated expectations, while valuations across semiconductors and AI infrastructure have compressed sharply.

We believe the combination of light positioning, returning corporate demand, persistent retail buying, and historically favorable post-midterm seasonality creates a compelling setup for US equities into year-end. With the election behind us and volatility potentially normalizing, there is considerable capacity for investors to rebuild risk.
